beats.name: Kenneth Colby
beats.role: Stanford psychiatrist who built PARRY to simulate paranoid schizophrenia

beats.text: PARRY modelled beliefs, judged new statements as fitting or threatening them, then chose how to respond.
beats.note: Contemporaries called it "ELIZA with attitude": a real conversational strategy, not just pattern-matched replies.

beats.lead: Psychiatrists tried to spot the computer. They mostly couldn't.
beats.text: In an early-1970s trial, experienced psychiatrists questioned real patients and PARRY over teleprinters; a separate panel of 33 psychiatrists then read the transcripts blind.
beats.note: Teleprinters, not chat windows: this predates the personal computer by nearly a decade.

beats.context: correct guesses at telling PARRY from a real patient, statistically no better than chance.

beats.text: PARRY and ELIZA even talked to each other over ARPANET at a 1972 computer conference.
beats.note: Two scripted programs, simulating a therapist and a patient, having a conversation neither could actually understand.

beats.line: A chatbot fooled psychiatrists in 1972, before the personal computer existed.
